title: Republicans delay vote on Trump’s US attorney general pick amid concerns
summary: Senate committee postpones vote as key Republican says he has not received information on 'anti-weaponisation' fund.
full_text:
Republicans delay vote on Trump’s US attorney general pick amid concerns
Senate committee postpones vote as key Republican says he has not received information on ‘anti-weaponisation’ fund.
Key Republicans have delayed a Senate committee vote on United States President Donald Trump’s pick to become attorney general.
The delay of the Judiciary Committee vote, which was originally set for Thursday, represents a major stumbling block in the nomination of Todd Blanche, who is currently leading the Department of Justice (DOJ) in an acting capacity.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items- list 1 of 3Trump halts $1.8bn ‘anti-weaponisation’ fund amid bipartisan backlash
- list 2 of 3Trump nominates Todd Blanche as US attorney general, teeing up Senate fight
- list 3 of 3California Governor Newsom says US Department of Justice investigating him
The decision came amid concerns from two key Republicans over Blanche’s proximity to Trump and, particularly, a controversial legal settlement in the president’s lawsuit against the top federal tax agency, the Internal Revenue Service (IRS). Blanche had served as Trump’s personal criminal defence lawyer before being tapped for the DOJ.
A spokesperson for the committee said late on Wednesday the vote would be postponed “as work continues to secure sufficient support” for Blanche.
All Republicans on the committee would need to vote in favour of Blanche to bring his nomination to a full vote in the chamber.
Republican Senators John Cornyn of Texas and Thom Tillis of North Carolina, who are leaving Congress, have been vocal in their scepticism over Blanche.
Their concerns have focused on Trump’s settlement with the IRS, following a lawsuit relating to an agency leak of Trump’s tax returns. The deal included a provision that shielded Trump and his family from future tax investigations. It also created a so-called $1.8bn “anti-weaponisation fund” under which individuals who alleged political prosecution by the federal government could seek compensation.
Both Republicans and Democrats vehemently opposed the fund, which they characterised as a scheme to use taxpayer funds to reward Trump’s allies.
During previous Senate hearings, Blanche has maintained that the plan was discontinued. A federal judge has also ruled the settlement illegal. Still, critics have said they have not received sufficient guarantees that the plan could not be resurrected, and have requested that Blanche and officials put their intention to abandon the settlement in writing.
Cornyn on Wednesday accused the DOJ of “stonewalling” further requests for information. He told reporters “the ball is in Blanche’s court”.
Trump, meanwhile, weighed in on the situation on Wednesday, suggesting Cornyn was holding up proceedings out of discontent with the president.
In May, Trump made the unexpected move of endorsing Cornyn’s Republican primary challenger, Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton. That came despite polls indicating that Cornyn, who has served in the Senate for more than two decades, would fare far better in the November race against Democratic candidate James Talarico.
Paxton went on to defeat Cornyn in the primary race.
“Maybe John Cornyn’s upset with me because I didn’t endorse him,” Trump told reporters on Wednesday.
On Thursday, Trump posted on Truth Social that he may withdraw Blanche’s nomination “temporarily”. He also criticised Cornyn and Tillis.
Trump wrote:”[Blanche] has the potential to go down as one of the Greatest Attorney Generals of All Time. However, John Cornyn, of Texas, and Thom Tillis, of North Carolina, both of whom I refused to Endorse, and whose political careers have been ended by my action, are refusing to vote for this Great Nominee, who will remain, in any event, as Acting. Remember, both Cornyn and Tillis voted for Merrick Garland, and others, too numerous to mention. I have no objection to temporarily withdrawing Todd’s name, if they do not do the right thing, and putting him back after Cornyn and Tillis are out of office.”
At the DOJ, Blanche has overseen many of Trump’s top priorities, including investigations and prosecutions into the president’s political enemies.
Still, under questioning from Senators this month, Blanche repeatedly maintained he oversaw the DOJ independently from the White House.
Blanche has also faced questioning over the DOJ’s handling of investigation files related to disgraced financier Jeffrey Epstein. The department was legally compelled by Congress to release those files earlier this year.

title: UEFA members vote to boycott FIFA if Infantino’s World Cup plans pursued
summary: European nations agree in virtual meeting to boycott FIFA competitions in protest at the private equity plan for World Cup.
full_text:
UEFA members vote to boycott FIFA if Infantino’s World Cup plans pursued
European nations agree in virtual meeting to boycott FIFA competitions in protest at private equity plan for World Cup.
European football’s governing body, UEFA, has voted to boycott FIFA events – including the World Cup – if the proposed sale of the event to private investors goes ahead.
The unanimous vote by UEFA member federations agreed on Thursday to boycott all FIFA competitions in protest against Gianni Infantino’s plan to sell stakes in the World Cup.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items- list 1 of 4What has FIFA charged Argentina with, and what could the punishment be?
- list 2 of 4Storm apologize after co-owner berates teen girls for support of Cunningham
- list 3 of 4South Africa’s le Clos breaks Commonwealth Games medal record
- list 4 of 4Viral finger-clicker suspended as cricket storm remains in global spotlight
“UEFA and its national associations will not participate in FIFA competitions,” the European football body said after an urgent online meeting of its 55 members.
The strategy meeting was called to counter FIFA President Infantino’s offer of $20m to each of its 211 global members, which must be accepted by mid-September.
Infantino’s secret proposal was revealed on Tuesday to spin off its commercial operations in a $20bn operation, with 20 percent owned by private investors.
The core investor would be a New York venture capital investment firm created by Joshua Kushner, the brother of US President Donald Trump’s son-in-law, Jared Kushner.
What did UEFA’s statement say after FIFA boycott vote?
“No UEFA national teams will participate in any FIFA competition for so long as these proposals remain alive, unless this proposal has been abandoned in its entirety and binding assurances have been given that FIFA will never again open its governance or competitions to private ownership,” UEFA said in a statement.
“The World Cup cannot be treated as an investment product. It is one of football’s greatest sporting legacies. It has been built over generations by players, national teams and supporters across every continent.
“No part of it should ever be surrendered to private investors. The World Cup is not for sale.”
The next FIFA competition is in Europe, the Women’s Under-20 World Cup hosted by Poland from September 5 .
What has been said elsewhere about FIFA’s World Cup plan?
Earlier on Thursday, Infantino called the plan to sell stakes in the World Cup a proposal but “not an obligation” after the idea provoked a furious response from football authorities around the globe.
Asian Football Confederation (AFC) President Sheikh Salman bin Ebrahim Al Khalifa branded FIFA’s lack of consultation over its plan as “totally unacceptable”, saying the move undermined the sport’s existing continental structure.
Former FIFA President Sepp Blatter slammed the football governing body’s plans, saying the tournament was not a commercial asset that belonged to a few executives.
“Football belongs to no individual and to no institution. It belongs to the people,” Blatter told the news agency Reuters on Wednesday.
FIFA have been contacted by Al Jazeera for a response to UEFA’s vote.

title: The economy slowed a bit -- but Americans continued to spend
summary: The U.S. economy grew at an annual rate of 1.5% in the spring, according to the Commerce Department. That's a modest slowdown from the previous quarter — but consumer spending picked up steam.
full_text:
The economy slowed a bit — but Americans continued to spend
The U.S. economy grew more slowly this spring than it did earlier in the year, but consumers continue to spend freely.
Gross domestic product — the broadest measure of economic activity — grew at an annual rate of 1.5% in April, May and June, according to a report Thursday from the Commerce Department. That's a modest slowdown from the first three months of the year when GDP grew at a 2.1% pace. A decline in government spending and a jump in imports, which count against the domestic tally, account for much of the change.
Consumer spending continues to power the economy, growing at a solid 2.1% pace during the second quarter. It's not clear how long shoppers can keep that up, however, in the face of rising prices.
Loading...
A separate report from the Commerce Department shows prices in June were up 3.7% from a year earlier. Inflation has been outpacing wage gains in recent months, forcing shoppers to dip into savings or borrow money to support their spending. The personal savings rate fell to 2.7% in June — a three year low.
The Commerce Department's inflation yardstick is closely watched by the Federal Reserve. Prices have been climbing faster than the central bank would like. But the Fed opted not to raise its benchmark interest rate on Wednesday.
Trade swings weighed on GDP during the quarter. Exports rose during the quarter, but imports rose faster.
"Trade has gone up and down and all around and clearly the tariffs are swinging things around," said Mark Zandi, chief economist at Moody's Analytics. "One quarter it might add to growth. The next quarter it might subtract from growth. Net over time, it's kind of sort of a wash."

BreakingChina voices ‘serious concern’ over new US curbs in senior trade talks
Beijing raises objections during a high-level call while both sides seek to build momentum ahead of an expected Xi-Trump summit
China on Thursday voiced “serious concern” over recent US economic restrictions during a video call between Vice-Premier He Lifeng, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer.
The exchange took place as both sides sought to finalise economic deliverables ahead of Chinese President Xi Jinping’s expected visit to the United States in September.
“The Chinese side expressed serious concern over the recent economic and trade restrictions imposed by the United States on China,” according to a readout by Chinese state news agency Xinhua.
The readout added that the two sides engaged in “candid, in-depth and constructive” exchanges, centred on implementing the “important consensus” reached at the Beijing meeting between US President Donald Trump and the Chinese leader.
Despite months of escalating trade tensions – including additional US tariffs, export controls and tit-for-tat restrictions targeting each other’s companies – both sides have continued engaging in an effort to secure outcomes ahead of the leaders’ summit.
On Tuesday, the Trump administration announced bans on imports of new Chinese robots and power inverters, citing threats to US national security and supply chain vulnerabilities.

full_text:
Top US science journals more likely to reject paper by Chinese authors: study
Even among American-based scientists, those with Chinese surnames had lower publication rates than those without, team finds
Researchers based in China or having a Chinese surname were far less likely than their US and Canadian counterparts to have papers published in the world’s most prestigious journals, according to a new study.
Just 2.5 per cent of submissions from China-based researchers were accepted, compared with 8.3 per cent overall for those from North America, a team found after analysing a rare dataset of more than 110,000 manuscripts submitted to Science and Science Advances between 2015 and 2020.
Even among US-based scientists, those with Chinese surnames had lower publication rates than those without Chinese surnames, they reported in Science Advances on July 15.
Sam Zhang, the study’s lead author and a computational social scientist at the University of Vermont, said one reason might be that China’s research system offered career and financial incentives for scientists to submit to elite journals such as Science.
That could encourage submissions even when some studies were not the best fit for the journals’ broad scientific scope.

Sam Mostyn says there is a widespread ‘failure to understand and engage with and feel proud of the very civic underpinnings of our democracy’

Australia faces a “growing catastrophe” from poor understanding of the country’s constitutional foundation, the governor general, Sam Mostyn, has warned as attacks on institutions and threats against elected officials undermine democratic participation.
Two years after her appointment as King Charles’s representative in Canberra, and as she brings a modern touch to the role of vice regal, Mostyn said that knowledge of how the country’s system of government operates was in steady decline and better civics education was needed.
“Where I see the most woeful lack of understanding … the basic understanding of the tenets of our democracy, is in the adult population,” Mostyn said.
“It’s mostly people who attack our system, who say we shouldn’t have a governor general, or who ask the governor general to do things that are not within my powers, or criticise me for signing the bills that I must sign, because they think I should have a view that clearly I do not have as governor general. Certain things I must do under my constitutional requirements.
“We’ve got a growing catastrophe, I think, in a failure to understand and engage with and feel proud of the very civic underpinnings of our democracy.”
In an interview for Guardian’s Australian Politics podcast, released on Friday, Mostyn said schoolchildren and newly sworn Australian citizens had the best understanding of how government and institutions worked.
The comments come as parliaments, the courts, the Australian Electoral Commission, and officeholders around the country face mounting criticism and abuse. Since the Covid pandemic, social media and online commentary has been identified as hotbed of corrosive sentiment, coinciding with rising threats against officials.
“It starts with understanding why we have a constitution, how it came to be,” Mostyn said of a potential solution.
“It’s 125 years old this year. It was built in a particular way, to bring the states and territories together, in order to build a sense of unity around the country, and it sets up everything that then builds the strength of our democracy.”
Mostyn said part of the problem was an absence of “a shared set of facts”, including in online discourse.
“I think this is a moment where it’s important for everyone, particularly people like me, in these offices, to keep up the project of why it matters that we show respect for each other, we learn to understand each other.
“There is a big risk that if we don’t, this is the beginning of the unraveling of social cohesion.”
The former businesswoman, AFL commissioner, political adviser and community leader has prioritised civics engagement and education in the role, bringing a less formal and more down-to-earth approach to the office of governor general. When she was appointed to the role – traditionally filled by former politicians, judges and military leaders – Mostyn promised an unstinting focus on kindness, on care and on respect.
Earlier this month, she hosted a roundtable on social cohesion and civics education with the Constitution Education Fund at her official residence in Canberra, Government House, attended by educators, public service leaders and thinktanks. Former high court chief justice Robert French is the fund’s chair.
Mostyn warned the types of people considering seeking political office in Australia is changing, because of sustained abuse and threats against elected representatives at all levels.
She said local councillors and mayors had told her public life was becoming difficult and increasingly unappealing.
“They [have] shared with me that lack of civility in their own communities, as directed to them as elected representatives, has become very very challenging, making it very difficult to seek office.
“If you know that you’re putting yourself into very dangerous traffic with people who now don’t feel the need to be respectful, who make direct threats … we’ve seen this all around the world with elected representatives at all levels.
“This desire to be hateful, to attack, to not enter into good, peaceful, robust but respectful discussions on things where we might not agree, and so that’s happening certainly in local government.”
Mostyn is the Crown’s representative in Australia, presides over the executive council, gives royal assent to legislation from parliament, appoints ministers and officials, dissolves parliament for elections and is the commander-in-chief of the Australian Defence Force.
She holds the reserve powers of the constitution, and attends and hosts hundreds of events every year, including for the Order of Australia.
In the past two years, Mostyn has used a growing social media presence to educate the public about the function of the governor general, and has conducted dozens of interviews, including with local media outlets when visiting far-flung communities.
In the wake of the Bondi beach terror attack in December last year, Mostyn immediately flew to Sydney to comfort victims and members of Australia’s Jewish community. At the height of the Socceroos World Cup campaign last month, she attended a Canberra pub to watch Australia play Paraguay in the middle of the day.
Speaking at Admiralty House, the governor general’s residence on Sydney Harbour, Mostyn revealed she had followed precedent from recent governors general and asked the Electoral Commissioner for an exemption from compulsory voting, preferring to be as removed as possible from political matters.
Her appointment to the role was not without controversy.
The Greens voted against legislation put to parliament to ensure Mostyn was paid the same amount as her predecessor. Gen David Hurley took a lower base salary due to his military pension.
Commentators criticised Mostyn’s qualifications, and said her high-profile positions on several issues including the voice to parliament referendum should have disqualified her from being appointed. One newspaper column called her “a governor-general from the Chairman’s Lounge.”
But Mostyn has confounded some critics in her first two years on the job.
In May, Chris Kenny, a columnist with the Australian newspaper lamented that too few commentators were ever prepared to admit when they were wrong about matters in public debate, acknowledging he had been mistaken in editorialising against Mostyn’s appointment on Sky News.
Kenny had argued her record could be “too political for Yarralumla”. But instead, Mostyn, he said, “has been diligent, dignified, hard-working and apolitical”.
The chief executive of the Constitution Education Fund, Kerry Jones, said Mostyn’s involvement could not be under stated.
“Probably the most important issue facing our country, our constitutional arrangements, our democracy, is that the people of Australia, the voters of Australia, seem to have lost a sense of trust in the institutions of government and the people in those institutions,” she said.
“If we survive – and when we look back on this period, which is being called a lack of social cohesion, or polarisation, or the rise of populism in politics and that is resulting in racism increasing again, and resulting in antisemitism and Islamophobia – the fact that the governor general is saying it is a crisis and we need to do something about it, could be seen as one of the most significant acts ever taken, I believe, by an Australian governor general for the good of Australia.”
Jones praised Mostyn’s energy and wisdom.
“She cares for every single Australian citizen in every community across Australia, and that radiates from everything she says.”
Mostyn said one of her guiding principles comes from the memoir of one of her predecessors, the academic and writer Sir Zelman Cowen.
Cowen served as governor general from 1977 until 1982, having replaced the controversial Sir John Kerr.

title: Icac revelations have left Angus Taylor’s colleagues anxious – and his factional enemies angry
summary:
The opposition leader is the highest-profile person mentioned so far at the NSW anti-corruption commission – and the political figure with the most to lose

  • Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

After the opening days of an inquiry exposing a dark underbelly of the New South Wales Liberals, the prevailing mood among Angus Taylor’s colleagues is one of apprehension.

The federal opposition leader is not a specific target of Operation Rosny, which is investigating allegations of corruption against people associated with the NSW branch. He is not accused of wrongdoing.

Continue reading...
full_text:
After the opening days of an inquiry exposing a dark underbelly of the New South Wales Liberals, the prevailing mood among Angus Taylor’s colleagues is one of apprehension.
The federal opposition leader is not a specific target of Operation Rosny, which is investigating allegations of corruption against people associated with the NSW branch. He is not accused of wrongdoing.
But Taylor is the highest-profile person mentioned so far – and the political figure with the most to lose.
To briefly recap, the opposition leader was on Tuesday named as a potential donor to the Reformers, a group of hard-right Liberal operatives plotting to take over the party from the inside.
The inquiry heard that a screenshot of a message from Dallas McInerney, then the chief executive of Catholic Schools NSW, was sent to Reformers members in which McInerney said he planned to “shake down Angus for 10k” during a breakfast meeting in Canberra.
The message was allegedly sent in March 2021 when Taylor was energy minister in the Morrison government.
Dylan Whitelaw, another Reformers associate who gave evidence on Tuesday and Wednesday, was read a later intercepted text message in which he claimed McInerney had told him he had secured a commitment from Taylor for a “15k injection and a 3k monthly donation!”
Whitelaw couldn’t recall sending the message and told the inquiry he would be “very surprised” if Taylor made any contribution.
After initially declining to refute the allegations, Taylor told a press conference on Wednesday that “no payment was made”.
“I’m not going to give a running commentary on all of this. I’m not a party to the proceedings, but no payment was made,” Taylor said.
If that response was supposed to put the matter to bed – and reassure his colleagues – it didn’t work.
On Thursday, Taylor was asked again about any potential donations during a press conference in Logan, Queensland.
“I’ve answered these questions yesterday. I’m not going to give a running commentary on it,” Taylor said.
“You can ask the question 100 times,” he repeated. “I’ll give you the same answer.”
Guardian Australia spoke with several Liberals on condition of anonymity, who believed Taylor must provide a more comprehensive answer, if indeed he had no role in bankrolling Reformers’ operations.
Unsurprisingly, the Labor treasurer, Jim Chalmers, expressed the same view.
“You know, I don’t want to interfere with the Icac process that his political allies are involved in at the moment … but there are a number of questions to be answered here, and he should front up and explain any involvement he’s had in this,” Chalmers said.
There were further questions for the opposition leader after Whitelaw was asked at Wednesday’s hearing if the $3,000 monthly payments that Taylor had allegedly agreed to were connected to a similar amount that Catholic Schools NSW was paying to the Reformers-linked lobbying firm Beckington.
There is no evidence that Taylor donated to the Reformers – only text messages suggesting payments would be sought or had been received.
He has not yet clarified what involvement – or even knowledge – he had of the Reformers and their alleged branch-stacking operation.
At Thursday’s hearing, Reformers witness Robert Assaf wasn’t sure what Taylor knew of their work but said he “definitely wasn’t opposed”.
Among the troves of text messages released by Icac is one from Whitelaw in which he told Reformers that “Angus Taylor is locked-in” for an event in Goulburn in September 2020.
An “Angus” is mentioned in several other text messages although the context is unclear.
There are, at this stage, more questions than answers. But the evidence so far has been enough to cause anxiety among his colleagues because of Taylor’s close ties to McInerney.
The pair are friends and factional allies. McInerney, one of the most powerful backroom operators in the NSW Liberal right faction, has helped Taylor with campaigns and was influential in his overthrowing of Sussan Ley.
The deeper Icac delves into McInerney’s dealings the more dangerous the inquiry becomes for Taylor, whose leadership is already tenuous given the Coalition’s dire position in the polls.
Liberals are surprised Taylor has not been quicker to distance himself from McInerney, who stepped down from Catholic Schools NSW after the inquiry was announced.
The opening days of evidence have elicited another emotion among Taylor’s factional enemies in NSW: anger.
The Reformers’ recruitment drives targeted, among others, branches in the federal seats of Berowra, Lindsay and Farrer, with the aim of dislodging Julian Leeser, Melissa McIntosh and Sussan Ley respectively.
McIntosh and Ley were only saved after an intervention from then prime minister Scott Morrison ahead of the 2022 federal election.
The notion that Taylor might have been supporting the plotters – potentially even financially – would amount to a level of treason well beyond what’s tolerated in the messy blood sport of factional politics.
The inquiry has more than seven weeks of hearings to go. Taylor might not be a target of Icac but he’s unlikely to emerge completely unscathed.

title: Firefighters race to extinguish blazes across EU as fire weather breaks records
summary:
European Forest Fire Information Service figures show conditions in EU 43% more severe than for same period in last 20 years

Fire weather in the EU has broken records for severity for this time of year, data shows, as firefighters race to extinguish blazes across the Mediterranean.

Inflamed by carbon pollution, the hot, dry and windy weather across the EU since the start of the year has been 43% more severe than the end-of-July average over the last two decades, data from the European Forest Fire Information Service (Effis) shows.

Continue reading...
full_text:
Fire weather in the EU has broken records for severity for this time of year, data shows, as firefighters race to extinguish blazes across the Mediterranean.
Inflamed by carbon pollution, the hot, dry and windy weather across the EU since the start of the year has been 43% more severe than the end-of-July average over the last two decades, data from the European Forest Fire Information Service (Effis) shows.
Three firefighters died in Greece on Tuesday, officials said, while firefighters in France and Spain made overnight progress tackling monster blazes that have burned dangerously close to large cities.
The figures, which were published on Thursday but may be revised further, showed that so far this year 435,000 hectares (1,075,000 acres) have burned, roughly triple the recent historical average. The devastation is the result of 1,400 fires, more than double the average.
In France, where a blaze in the dense pine forests near Bordeaux grew so big it generated a rare thunderstorm that could ignite more fires, a total of 91,000 hectares have burned, according to Effis, breaking the country’s record for a full year of fires – with one month of summer still to go.
Regional authorities in Gironde said the fire remained under control after a quiet night, with work continuing around its edge and in active hotspots. They said temperatures on Thursday had been expected to be “fairly favourable” after Wednesday’s 38C heat and strong winds hampered firefighting efforts.
They allowed a further 84,000 people to return home on Thursday, after 60,000 people were given the green light on Tuesday.
In Spain, which experienced its largest wildfire on record, west of Madrid, a total of 207,000 hectares have burned across the country, according to Effis. The figure is nearly five times the average for this time of year but shy of the devastation reached by late July during the 2022 fires.
Regional authorities in Madrid said the fire situation had been declared “stable” but residents of seven housing estates were unable to return home. Pedro Sánchez, the prime minister, announced the end of the national emergency in the regions of Ávila and Madrid on Thursday morning.
However, a new fire near the Portuguese border prompted the evacuation of 600 people, officials said. Aemet, the Spanish meteorological agency, said temperatures above 35C were expected on Thursday in large areas of the interior, with some regions bracing for highs of 40C-42C.
Wildfires in France and Spain have forced more than 300,000 people from their homes and tourist accommodation this month, prompting both countries to request EU support in the form of firefighters, fire engines, and water-dropping planes and helicopters.
Ursula von der Leyen, the president of the European Commission, thanked firefighters for their “courage and commitment” on Wednesday as crews sent by Romania and Greece extended their stays. “As the fires in France and Spain continue to ravage, European solidarity knows no limit,” she said.
Futher difficult weeks were expected as fires worsened in Italy and Greece, officials at the EU’s crisis management centre said on Wednesday morning. Later that day, the Greek fire department announced the deaths of two firefighters who were tackling a blaze on the island of Crete, and of another in the south of the mainland.
Greece has so far had a relatively calm fire season, Effis data up to 29 July shows, with slightly fewer fires than usual and a burned area well below the average.
Meanwhile, Italy and Portugal have seen near-record breaking numbers of fires, and burned areas well above average. The countries have so far been spared the scale of destruction experienced by France and Spain, but one firefighter died in Italy last week while tackling blazes in Sicily.
Climate breakdown is causing Europe to burn this summer, with a series of almost back-to-back heatwaves drying out vegetation which then provides a vast fuel surplus that has allowed small fires to grow into raging infernos.
Sánchez repeated calls to create a “national pact” to address the climate emergency during a visit to a command post on Wednesday.
“These fires may or may not be caused by humans, but in any case, they increase exponentially as a result of these high temperatures, low humidity, and also the atmospheric phenomena that these fires, these large fires, cause in our forests,” he said.
A study by an international team of scientists, published in the journal Scientific Reports, found that since the 1980s, the number of fires in southern Europe and the area burned had steadily declined as authorities became better at preventing and suppressing them.
The study, published on Thursday, found the trend began to reverse in 2018. It found that summer days conducive to strong wildfires had more than doubled since 1981 across large parts of Portugal, Spain, France, Italy and Greece; in parts of France and Spain, the summertime fire weather index over the last decade was up to 50% higher than the 1981-2010 average.
The scientists said this had resulted in European fires shifting to “fewer, but more intense and larger events”, with fires that escaped initial attacks by firefighters able to “quickly become catastrophic”.
José Miguel Viñas, a meteorologist at the forecaster Meteored, who was not involved in the research, said it scientifically demonstrated a fact that southern Europe and other parts of the world had observed in recent years.
“Increasingly extreme conditions of heat, dryness and wind are fuelling large forest fires,” he said. “Once started, they spread rapidly and become uncontrollable, overwhelming the firefighting efforts.”
Rapid analyses have found western Europe’s June heatwave would have been “virtually impossible” in a world without climate breakdown, while the level of soil dryness – a major factor in bigger blazes – is five times more likely than it would be in a climate 1.4C cooler. The heatwaves are estimated to have killed at least 10,000 people and cost grain farmers €2bn (£1.7bn) in lost crops.
The increase in temperatures from fossil fuel pollution has come as rural regions in southern Europe have hollowed out, with farms being abandoned as populations age and young people move to cities. The resultant overgrowth in vegetation has troubled firefighters and wildfire researchers across the Mediterranean.

title: Iran’s war with the US is not its only conflict as internal crises mount
summary:
Government fears social discontent on ‘most important battlefield’ of economy and livelihoods as war takes its toll amid anti-state dissent

  • Middle East crisis live – latest updates

Iran, in the midst of an escalating five-month war with the US, continues to stumble from one internal crisis to another – whether it is over public executions, the rising cost of living, the alleged bias of the state broadcaster or even the post-midnight destruction of pavements outside liberal-leaning Tehran cafes. Very little that happens in Iran, cultural or political, momentous or trivial, does so uncontested.

But there is now a growing threat of a long diplomatic deadlock, forged by mutual distrust in which neither side believes the other will stick to any agreement. That impasse has occurred as the war broadens, drawing in Yemen, Iraq and now Egypt. In Iran, at least, the advocates of escalation are winning. As a result, a convergence of Iran’s conflicts, internal and external, becomes more likely.

Continue reading...
full_text:
Iran, in the midst of an escalating five-month war with the US, continues to stumble from one internal crisis to another – whether it is over public executions, the rising cost of living, the alleged bias of the state broadcaster or even the post-midnight destruction of pavements outside liberal-leaning Tehran cafes. Very little that happens in Iran, cultural or political, momentous or trivial, does so uncontested.
But there is now a growing threat of a long diplomatic deadlock, forged by mutual distrust in which neither side believes the other will stick to any agreement. That impasse has occurred as the war broadens, drawing in Yemen, Iraq and now Egypt. In Iran, at least, the advocates of escalation are winning. As a result, a convergence of Iran’s conflicts, internal and external, becomes more likely.
Parts of the Trump administration and the Iranian opposition – including Reza Pahlavi, the son of the former deposed Shah – have never abandoned the belief that the Iranian government is on the brink of collapse.
What is true is that the picture of cohesive if brittle society presented by the millions attending the funeral of the supreme leader Ali Khamenei earlier this month revealed only one side of the public mood.
‘We just practice enduring’
Masoud Pezeshkian, Iran’s president, rarely tires of warning that the conditions that led to the bloody protests in January remain.
At a recent meeting of the supreme judicial council he argued: “Iran is engaged in a full-scale war. Today’s war is not just a war of missiles; the enemy has come to the conclusion that it cannot force the Iranian nation to surrender through military attacks. The most important battlefield today is the economy and livelihood of the people. If economic pressures cause social discontent to form and this discontent spreads, the enormous social capital that the people have created in support of the system will be lost.”
Undoubtedly dissent, in the form of despair, exists.
Golshan Fathi, a Tehran human rights activist, recently wrote on her social media page: “The same sick cycle repeats … morning … the call to prayer, news of an execution … noon with power cuts, afternoon the water stops … dusk, the anxiety of war and renewed attacks on cities, and at midnight, the earth trembles.
“And tomorrow, the same story again. Caught between natural disasters, management failures, and man-made crises … every day we don’t live, we just practice enduring. Repetition, repetition, repetition … until a weary land no longer asks, ‘What will tomorrow bring?’ It just waits to see, ‘When will the next crisis arrive?’”
Dissent in the form of political protest also exists, whether it is those inside jails or citizens in the squares of Isfahan protesting against the current wave of intimidatory public executions. Many critics ask why the punishment of the accused takes place in public gallows, yet their trials are held in secret courts.
On Monday the political bureau of the Nation’s Union party warned that ignoring the protests over the wave of executions could have “devastating consequences”, and urged academics and religious scholars to intervene to end this state violence.
‘War has no winners’
Azar Mansouri, once a close reformist ally of Pezeshkian, warned last week at the annual meeting of the Iranian reformist front about a small but vocal group that seemed determined to portray negotiated agreements with the US as retreats or defeat. War, she warned, “is not just a confrontation between military forces and armies. It is the destruction of the economy, the erosion of social capital, the spread of despair, the emigration of elites, the increase in poverty and the loss of opportunities for development. Ultimately, it threatens the future of the nation.”
Similarly a “we do not want war” statement signed by 268 political activists this month said they believed the overwhelming majority opposed war, and this should be tested in a public vote. Another letter from 1,000 activists linked with the former president Mohammad Khatami warned “the contemporary experience of Iran is that war has no winners. Those who advocate negotiations should not be slandered.”
What unites these initiatives is a fear that diplomats are losing, and Iran is being edged into a forever war that can be portrayed as an Iranian-Arab war, a war that would be to Israel’s advantage.
Yet opposition to the whole principle of negotiation with America – fuelled by Donald Trump’s own erratic behaviour – is being voiced by hardliners, in street rallies and more recently on unofficial billboards.
The sway of the hardliners lies less in their strength in parliament – many were elected on low turnouts and anyway have been deposed from key committees in parliament – but in the belief a network of deep-state support exists in the military and in the office of the supreme leader, Mojtaba Khamenei. The absence of Khamenei from public view makes it harder to resolve the controversy about whether the family see any purpose in negotiations with America.
The closure of cafes, or the destruction of the sidewalks around them, is also seen as a crude attempt to shape debate. Last year the prominent hardliner Saeed Jalili described the cafes as an anti-Islamic “third space” beyond the dormitory or the office where people go to escape loneliness. “In this concept the family loses any meaning. This stands in opposition to Islam’s philosophy of marriage.”
Alleged broadcaster bias
Despite being a conservative newspaper, Jomhouri-e Eslami complained “an addiction to violating the dignity of one’s political opponents is increasing every day”. That in turn is, in part, a reference to the criticism of negotiators meted out by the publicly funded national broadcaster IRIB, long seen as a preserve of those opposed to talks with the west. Many see IRIB as an exclusive platform for the hardliners rather than a mirror of a diverse society.
The crisis between the government and the broadcaster is now out in the open after interventions by Pezeshkian and Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, the chief negotiator, were censored.
The government in a statement complained: “Censorship of the president’s speech, unilateral destruction of the government’s performance, and efforts to destroy the memorandum of understanding that was formed to get the country through the crisis and protect national interests are no longer media criticism; they are a stand against national cohesion, empathy, and unity.
“The question is clear: is the Iranian broadcasting system with the people, government, and interests of Iran or with those who benefit from division, tension, and polarisation? The national media should be the voice of Iranian unity, not a platform for destroying the government and disrupting national understanding.”
There are calls for a complete overhaul of the organisation’s accountability when a new head is appointed this September. At one level the politics of the national broadcaster should not matter, since surveys suggest less than 12% of the country watch it. The difficulty for the government is that this leaves audiences watching hostile foreign satellite channels instead.
Economic toll of war
This tension over the national broadcaster coincides with a period of unprecedented economic pressure. In the next six months food rationing might become necessary, Majid-Reza Hariri, the head of the Iran-China chamber of commerce, warned this week. Gholamhossein Mohammadi, the deputy minister of labour, said more than a million jobs had been lost as a result of the war.
In a way rationing – through food price inflation – has already started as Iranians are being forced to change their diets due to the cost of fruit, eggs and chicken. title: Russian Bombardment Kills at Least Eight in Ukraine as Zelensky Renews Plea for Air Defense Supplies
summary: "Untimely assistance and delays in the delivery of anti-ballistic missiles lead to this kind of destruction," said Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky.
full_text:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said Russia launched over 70 missiles and 280 drones in an overnight attack on Ukraine that killed at least eight people, including three children, and left dozens injured.
Kyiv, the Ukrainian capital, and the western city of Lviv, near the Poland border, were most impacted, local officials reported.
“Dozens of ordinary homes, civilian businesses, and infrastructure facilities were destroyed and damaged,” said Zelensky on Thursday, as he decried the “critical shortage of air defense missiles from our partners” and called for assistance from other countries.
“All partners know how and with what they can help. Untimely assistance and delays in the delivery of anti-ballistic missiles lead to this kind of destruction, these kinds of casualties that, unfortunately, we are seeing today,” Zelensky added, doubling down on his previous statements on the perils of delayed defensive equipment.
Zelensky shared a series of images and videos that showed buildings reduced to rubble and emergency services carrying out search and rescue operations.
"This Russian terror once again proves that protection against the Russian missile threat is the most important task when it comes to saving the lives of our people," Zelensky declared.
The Russian Defense Ministry said its strikes targeted Ukrainian air bases, arms factories, and military telecommunications and logistics facilities.
Following the attack, Ukraine’s air force said it shot down just one of nine ballistic missiles sent into its airspace.
Zelensky has repeatedly appealed for more U.S.-made Patriot missile interceptors as they are capable of downing Russia’s ballistic missiles, but there’s a critical short supply.
At the NATO summit in Ankara, Turkey, earlier this month, U.S. President Donald Trump told Zelensky that the U.S. would extend Ukraine a license to manufacture Patriot missile interceptors.
The pair met again for a closed-door meeting in the Oval Office on Tuesday, sharing what Zelensky described afterward as a “good” sit-down.
They “discussed licenses for Patriot interceptor production and several other ideas that could help,” according to the Ukrainian leader, but no concrete details or next steps for manufacturing plans have been released.
During his time in Washington, Zelensky watched from inside the chamber as the U.S. Senate advanced a bill that would impose tougher sanctions on Russia.
Elsewhere, the European Commission stepped up its support for Ukraine, announcing Thursday it would disburse a further €3.47 billion (around $3.99 billion) for drones, missiles, air defense, and fighter jets under its €90 billion Ukraine Support Loan.
Ukraine’s new Prime Minister Sergii Koretskyi expressed gratitude, saying the “funds will strengthen our defense and help finance Ukraine’s most urgent needs.”
Zelensky later held a meeting with Ukraine’s new military chief Mykhailo Drapatyi and other defense officials to discuss the country’s challenges facing Russia’s ballistic missile attacks and its “ability to counter this tactic, both at the military and diplomatic levels.”
Russian missile "violated" airspace in Poland, says Tusk
Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said "during the Russian massive missile attack on western Ukraine, a violation of Polish airspace occurred."
He convened a “coordination team” early Thursday morning to assess the site where the projectile fell.
“I am in contact with the leaders of European countries regarding the violation of Polish airspace. Everyone declares full solidarity and readiness for any assistance,” Tusk added.
The leader of Poland, a NATO member, later said in a press conference that “there is no reason to believe that Poland was the target,” but maintained a violation had taken place.
“After my conversation with President Zelensky, it is quite clear to me that the next 100 days could decide the outcome of this war,” Tusk, who met with Zelensky on Wednesday, declared. “Right now, I would say the chances are fifty-fifty. Much depends on decisions made by the President of the United States.”
NATO is “in close contact with the Polish authorities about the violation of Poland’s airspace,” NATO spokesperson for the Supreme Headquarters Allied Powers Europe (SHAPE) Col. Martin O’Donnell told TIME in an emailed statement.
“The Supreme Allied Commander Europe (SACEUR), General Alexus G. Grynkewich, spoke earlier today with Poland's Chief of Defence General Wiesław Kukułan about NATO and Poland’s response to the incident, which remains under investigation,” the statement continued. “SACEUR underlined that NATO will continue to take all necessary measures to defend NATO territory.”
European leaders denounce Russian aggression against Ukraine
European officials were quick to denounce the overnight bombardment against Ukraine and the reported violation of Polish airspace.
“France condemns in the strongest possible terms the Russian strikes that killed civilians in Ukraine, as well as the violation of Polish airspace,” said French President Emmanuel Macron. “Our support for Ukraine and our allies will not waver. This is a matter of our collective security.”
European Council president António Costa echoed those remarks, warning that the incident underscored a broader threat posed by Russia.
“Last night, Russia launched a massive combined strike against Ukraine. During the attack, Polish airspace was also violated, underlining once again that Russia’s aggression is a threat to the security of Europe as a whole,” he said.
European Commission president Ursula von der Leyen labeled the attack “another unacceptable violation of our E.U. airspace caused by Russia’s latest strikes on Ukraine.”
“To put an end to this, we are helping Ukraine win this war in every way we can. And we are building a robust European security architecture on land, at sea and in the air,” she said.
This is not the first time Russia has reportedly violated the airspace of a NATO member.
In late May, a Russian strike hit an apartment building in eastern Romania—a crash E.U. leaders referred to as “a serious violation of Romania’s sovereignty and European airspace.”

title: GPU Management: Why Idle GPUs Are the New Grounded Aircraft
full_text:
GPU Management: Why Idle GPUs Are the New Grounded Aircraft
Utilization, not intelligence, is the next real constraint in AI.
Aviation learned this the hard way. For most of the industry's history, the number that best predicted whether an airline would survive was how much of the day each aircraft spent on the ground.
The reason is structural. An aircraft's costs accrue by the calendar hour: financing, depreciation, hull insurance, scheduled maintenance, crew contracts. Its revenue accrues only by the flight hour. Every hour spent on the ground shrinks the output side of that equation while the cost side keeps running exactly as before. Utilization also sits downstream of almost everything else an airline does. Turnaround discipline, network design, maintenance planning, crew rostering, and spare parts availability all eventually show up in that one number, because a broken operation underneath it keeps planes on the ground no matter what else goes right.
A bigger fleet still helps. More aircraft means more available capacity, plainly and simply. But two airlines flying comparable fleets on comparable routes can end up with very different economics, and most of that gap traces back to one measurement rather than fleet size.
Enterprise AI is running into the same structure, on a different piece of hardware. A GPU accrues cost by the calendar hour too, through financing, depreciation, power, and cooling, whether or not it's doing anything useful in a given moment. Its output only accrues by the compute hour. More GPUs helps in roughly the way a bigger fleet helps an airline: real capacity, a genuine advantage, and still no guarantee of the result that actually decides who wins. Two companies with comparable GPU budgets increasingly diverge based on how much of that hardware is doing something useful at any given moment, not on how much of it either one owns. That same number, like an airline's utilization rate, sits downstream of nearly every other infrastructure decision a company makes. Intelligence has carried the industry this far. Utilization is where the next real constraint is forming.
The Bottleneck Moved From Models to Compute
The scarcity didn't disappear as AI scaled. It moved up the chain, landing on a different resource entirely.
The first wave of enterprise AI was won on model quality. Bigger models, trained on more compute, evaluated against tougher benchmarks: parameter count and leaderboard position dominated the conversation, and the race produced models genuinely good enough to run real enterprise workloads. That capability arrives bundled with a dependency, though. Production AI runs on specialized hardware, and today that hardware is almost entirely GPUs.
GPUs are expensive, supply constrained, and in demand far beyond what's available, and this holds even at the very top of the market. In 2020, Microsoft built OpenAI a dedicated supercomputer: over 10,000 GPUs and 285,000 CPU cores, reported at the time as one of the five largest systems in the world, assembled to train what became GPT-3. At the time, it looked like an almost unimaginable concentration of hardware, the kind of number that made compute look like a solved problem for whoever could get access to it. Six years later, that number reads more like a starting point than a ceiling. By 2026, even the best capitalized labs on the planet were treating compute access as a live strategic constraint rather than a settled one. Anthropic alone was running simultaneous multi-gigawatt commitments across four separate hardware platforms, Amazon, Google, Microsoft, and AMD, layered within months of one another, while Meta signed a comparable multi-gigawatt deal of its own. Spreading commitments across four vendors at once is what compute scarcity looks like when a buyer has effectively unlimited capital and still can't get enough from any single source.
Six years apart, both events marked the frontier of what a lab needed just to stay competitive. What changed in between has less to do with AI getting more capable, and everything to do with capability no longer being the binding constraint.
The same pattern shows up downstream of the labs, in a different form. Enterprises consuming these models through an API run into a pricing problem more than a hardware one. Cost scales linearly with tokens used, and that single fact separates the economics of a proof of concept from the economics of production almost completely. A PoC processing a few thousand requests a month looks affordable. The same workload at production volume can turn into a cost line that never quite clears. The alternative gaining ground is straightforward enough: enterprises acquiring their own GPUs and running models locally, trading a variable, linearly scaling cost for a fixed capital one.
API cost rises with usage, while owned infrastructure stays close to fixed. Past the breakeven point, the trade reverses.
That shift turns the GPU into infrastructure rather than a line item, sized for growth, sized for demand peaks, and therefore sized above what any given week actually needs. Which means the purchase doesn't close the problem. It opens a new one. The day the cluster comes online, the question stops being can we get accelerators and becomes can we keep them busy, and only the first question had a procurement team assigned to it. Signing for the hardware is the part with a deadline and an owner. Keeping it off the ground is the part that quietly decides whether the deal was worth signing.
These deals describe capacity commitments, not efficiency. How well that capacity gets used is a separate question, owned by different people, measured far less rigorously, and considerably further from being solved.
Why Busy Clusters Still Waste Capacity
A cluster full of busy GPUs can still be wasting most of its potential, and the reason is almost always the same one. GPUs run continuously, day and night, while the demand placed on them does not. Infrastructure has to be sized for the peak, the moment training runs, batch jobs, and real time traffic all land at once, which leaves a meaningful share of capacity provisioned and unused outside that peak. Better forecasting could solve that on its own if every GPU could absorb every kind of work equally well. Few can, and that turns out to be the harder half of the problem.
The mismatch begins one layer deeper.
In the first generation of enterprise AI, a GPU's job was largely singular: run inference. Today the same hardware supports training, fine-tuning, quantization, real-time inference, batch inference, embedding generation, and model evaluation, often for the same organization, sometimes for the same model, on the same cluster. Each of these workloads wants something different from the hardware, and the differences run deep. Real-time inference needs low latency above nearly everything else, because a slow response counts as a failed one. Batch work cares about throughput and tolerates delay, sometimes for hours. Training can occupy a GPU continuously for a stretch measured in hours or days. Quantization needs a large amount of capacity, but only briefly. A scheduler tuned for one of these will misallocate the other three almost by default. The failure doesn't always show up on a utilization dashboard either. A cluster can report high average occupancy while several queued jobs wait for a GPU shape that happens to be busy running something else entirely.
The exact workload mix varies by organization. The shape of the problem does not. This is also where the aircraft analogy runs into its limit, and the limit teaches something rather than just qualifying the comparison. An idle aircraft can usually be redeployed to any route in the fleet: a 737 sitting in Chicago can fly to Denver instead of Dallas without much penalty. An idle GPU can only absorb a workload whose memory, latency, and duration profile it can actually serve. That difference makes orchestration harder than fleet

Do you remember Friend? The Friend that launched an AI pendant, spent $1.8 million of its $2.5 million to acquire friend.com, and plastered the NYC subway with ads promoting artificial companionship?
Friend re-launches its AI pendant with a speaker that talks to you, for twice the price
Everyone hated it, so Friend is making it even more expensive.
Everyone hated it, so Friend is making it even more expensive.
Yeah well, if you didn’t remember, Friend is back. And now, it’s twice the price.
This morning, Friend launched a new ad showing two people talking to their Friend pendants about very personal life problems. It didn’t say it explicitly, but the ad showcased a new feature the pendant now includes: a speaker. Before, Friend would only message back to you, but now, it will talk to you, too. For some reason, the addition of that feature is apparently worth $120, as the originally $129 product now costs $249.
The re-launch comes about nine months after a large Friend protest took place in NYC, where protestors tried to bring attention to our growing dependance on technology. Friend was the obvious target, considering it had spend a boatload of money advertising throughout the city. Its founder, Avi Schiffmann, even posted an image promoting the protest, and showed up to it himself.
Shiffmann posted a tweet of the new ad, calling it “Friend 2.0,” even though the product is still just called “Friend” on its site. I’m sure things will go much better this time.

full_text:
The SkyNomad N90 Max is the latest electric SUV from Xiaomi and its first extended-range EV, with a claimed range of over 1,705 km (about 1,059 miles). It will come in both five- and seven-seat configurations, as well as an N90 Max Camping Edition.
Xiaomi’s SkyNomad N90 Max is an extended-range EV with a transforming interior
It’s got swiveling seats, footrests, and there’s even a camper model with a pop-up top.
It’s got swiveling seats, footrests, and there’s even a camper model with a pop-up top.
One of the big features of the N90 is its highly customizable interior. The front seats rotate 180 degrees, the center armrest slides out to become a small table, and the second row features zero gravity seats with footrests. The Camping Edition adds a pop-up top, a rooftop bed platform, an attachment point for a tent, and a detachable table. Some models will also include a fridge and overhead speakers. Xiaomi is pitching the N90 as a sort of living space on wheels, saying it can be a “studio for one, a cafe for two, a lounge for three, a playground for the whole family.”
The company also unveiled the smaller SkyNomad N70 and N70 Max, which seat five but are built on the same extended range technology platform.

title: Razer’s new keyboards drop the price on powerful gaming features
summary: Razer has insisted that optical keyboard switches are the best choice for competitive esports stars and the sweatiest of try-hards, but it's now relenting slightly by offering cheaper keyboards with magnetic switches and a similar array of gaming features. The $120 Razer Huntsman V3 HE Magnetic Mini and $140 Huntsman V3 HE Magnetic Tenkeyless, both […]
full_text:
Razer has insisted that optical keyboard switches are the best choice for competitive esports stars and the sweatiest of try-hards, but it’s now relenting slightly by offering cheaper keyboards with magnetic switches and a similar array of gaming features. The $120 Razer Huntsman V3 HE Magnetic Mini and $140 Huntsman V3 HE Magnetic Tenkeyless, both launching today, are the company’s first keyboards to use Hall effect switches. They’re wired-only boards loaded with gaming-first features, and I’ve had a brief chance to test both and take them for a spin.
Razer’s new keyboards drop the price on powerful gaming features
The Huntsman V3 HE Magnetic TKL and Mini look like most other Razer boards (a little ugly), but they’re loaded up with competitive gaming tech.
The Huntsman V3 HE Magnetic TKL and Mini look like most other Razer boards (a little ugly), but they’re loaded up with competitive gaming tech.
The new Huntsman boards offer the hallmarks found in many other Hall effect mechanical keyboards, like programmable actuation points, faster key releases with Rapid Trigger, and an 8KHz polling rate. Their linear switches have an average latency of 0.6ms, which is of course very fast but ever-so-slightly slower than the 0.48ms of optical Huntsman boards like the V3 Pro. Razer can stand by its claim that optical analog boards are faster, but we’re really splitting hairs here.
The new magnetic models offer plenty of speed at significantly lower prices, as the optical Huntsman Pro boards start at $220, and they have Razer’s full arsenal of deeply customizable gaming features. This includes things like Snap Tap, which prioritizes your last movement input on the A or W keys and makes for easier counter-strafing (considered cheating by some and banned by Valve); Snap Flex, for setting up keys to trigger specific actions upon release; and Dual-Keypress Priority, preventing an accidental movement input from interrupting two previously held keys (like diagonal movement). Those last two features are also available on the mid-range optical Huntsman V3 Tenkeyless 8KHz, and coming to the higher-end Huntsman V3 Pros via firmware update.
Do these all sound like pretty niche features for specialized use cases? They are. While these cheaper keyboards are designed to appeal to a wider audience, these kinds of features are designed for the most competitive of online shooters — specifically, games with nuances to their movement techniques, like Counter-Strike 2. Razer is primarily competing with Wooting, Asus, and SteelSeries in this space, going feature-for-feature to cater to this hardcore subset of gamers. Wooting’s 80HE and 60HE v2 are some of the most praised gaming keyboards around, but Razer’s new HE boards undercut them by about $60.
I spent some time testing both the 65-percent and TKL versions of the new HE Huntsman pair, and since my Counter-Strike days are long behind me, these keyboards feel more than fast enough for any speedy inputs my aging fingers can muster. There is obviously not much reason to buy either of these boards unless you primarily care about their deep-in-the-weeds gaming features and making detailed customizations in Razer’s software (especially since entry-level mechanicals have gotten so good). The Razer Synapse app is as burdensome as ever, but you can also use a web version if you don’t need to make frequent changes or just don’t want to deal with it constantly running.
Razer’s doubleshot PBT keycaps have a nicely textured feel that’s more coarse than typical keycaps, but boy, do I dislike these shine-through legends. Some lettering and symbols are oddly proportioned and ugly, making an otherwise simple-looking floating keycap design look basic. The plastic base sitting beneath the aluminum top case makes these keyboards pretty light and portable, but the combination feels a bit cheap compared to full-metal keyboards. And there are no added conveniences like a volume knob, included wrist rest, or status screen like on the Huntsman Pro models.
But the magnetic Huntsman pair both sound much better to my ears than Razer’s pricier models. The new HE keyboards create a nice clacky tone, while the Huntsman V3 Pro is louder and clunkier sounding. (I’ve got a high tolerance for noisy keyboards, but the latter can get on my nerves after typing for a while.) Preferred typing sounds are pretty subjective, but as improved as Razer’s new HE boards are in the sound department, I’ve tested other 8K wired Hall effect keyboards that are much more pleasing to the ears.
For the same price of Huntsman V3 HE, you can get more unique looking and nicer sounding keyboards, but if your sole focus is competitive gaming, these new models are a good value compared to other popular (and pricier) boards. Enjoy your speedy keys and all the RGB lighting your heart desires. Just don’t get banned.
Photography by Antonio G. Di Benedetto / The Verge

title: Global banks test tokenized money for cross-border payments in $1 million BIS pilot
full_text:
Global banks test tokenized money for cross-border payments in $1 million BIS pilot
Twenty-eight banks, including JPMorgan, Citi and UBS, moved real money across borders in a live test of blockchain-based settlement.
- A group of major lenders settled real cross-border payments using tokenized central bank reserves and commercial bank deposits across six currencies in a major test of the technology stack.
- The test processed about $1 million in transfers through 30 transactions that settled in roughly 80 seconds on a shared ledger, improving traceability while operating alongside existing payment systems.
- By enabling simultaneous foreign-exchange settlement and a single shared record of ownership, the project aims to reduce risks and costs in cross-border payments as part of a broader shift toward tokenized financial assets.
Some of the world's biggest banks have completed real cross-border payments using tokenized money in a test led by the Bank for International Settlements (BIS), another sign that tokenization is moving into the plumbing of global finance.
Project Agorá, which brings together five central banks and 28 commercial lenders including JPMorgan, Citi, UBS, Deutsche Bank and Standard Chartered, processed roughly $1 million (CHF 800,000) in real-value transactions across six currencies — the U.S. dollar, euro, British pound, Japanese yen, Swiss franc and South Korean won.
The pilot used tokenized central bank reserves and commercial bank deposits to settle corporate, interbank payments perand foreign exchange settlements. The payments settled in an average of about 80 seconds, even though the prototype was not directly integrated with banks' existing payment infrastructure, the BIS report said.
The project fits into a broader shift as stablecoins and tokenized assets gain traction across global finance. Asset managers have begun issuing tokenized money market and private credit funds, while stablecoins are increasingly being used for cross-border payments and corporate treasury operations.
A new model for cross-border payments
Project Agorá explores whether the same technology can modernize the infrastructure banks use to move money internationally.
Unlike stablecoins, which are typically issued by the private sector like Circle (CRCL) and Tether, the BIS’ Project Agorá tokenizes two forms of traditional bank money: central bank reserves used by commercial banks to settle with one another, and commercial bank deposits held by customers.
Today's cross-border payments often pass through multiple correspondent banks, with each institution maintaining its own records before funds are finally settled. The BIS pilot instead placed tokenized money on a shared ledger, allowing banks to complete transactions while sharing a single record of ownership and payment status.
The project also tested foreign exchange payments, allowing banks to exchange two currencies at the same time instead of waiting for one side of the transaction to settle before completing the other. That reduces the risk of one party sending money without receiving the other currency in return.
The banks involved also said the platform made it easier to track payments from start to finish and worked alongside existing payment systems instead of replacing them.

title: Aviva Investors launches tokenized fund after Central Bank of Ireland approval
summary: The new XRPL-based share class gives eligible investors blockchain-based access to a regulated US dollar liquidity fund while keeping traditional custody arrangements.
full_text:
Aviva Investors launches tokenized fund after Central Bank of Ireland approval
The new XRPL-based share class gives eligible investors blockchain-based access to a regulated US dollar liquidity fund while keeping traditional custody arrangements.
Aviva Investors, the London-based asset management arm of Aviva Plc, has launched a tokenized share class of its US Dollar Liquidity Fund on the XRP Ledger (XRPL) after receiving approval from the Central Bank of Ireland, marking another step in the growth of tokenized real-world assets.
The company announced that the tokenized share class will be available to eligible investors with digital wallets. The fund’s underlying assets will continue to be held by custodian BNY Mellon, while Komainu will provide digital asset custody and Licuido will supply the tokenization infrastructure.
The US Dollar Liquidity Fund invests in high-grade, short-term US dollar-denominated debt securities and money market instruments issued by governments, banks and corporations. According to Aviva, the tokenized share class offers the same investment objective and liquidity profile as the conventional fund.
The launch follows Aviva Investors’ partnership tie-up with Ripple, announced earlier this year. Ripple’s XRP Ledger provides the blockchain infrastructure for issuing and managing the tokenized shares.
Aviva’s fund joins a growing list of tokenized investment products on public blockchains. On XRPL, it follows Archax’s tokenization of UK asset manager abrdn’s US Dollar Liquidity Fund in 2024. More broadly, traditional asset managers including BlackRock, Franklin Templeton and Apollo have also launched tokenized funds as demand for blockchain-based financial products continues to expand.

title: Canadian crypto ownership increases to 25%: Ontario survey
summary: A survey of more than 2,000 Canadians in late 2025 and early 2026 showed an increasing awareness of risk around the crypto industry and higher ownership of assets.
full_text:
Canadian crypto ownership increases to 25%: Ontario survey
A survey of more than 2,000 Canadians in late 2025 and early 2026 showed an increasing awareness of risk around the crypto industry and higher ownership of assets.
Canadians’ ownership of cryptocurrencies increased to 25% in 2026 from 10% in 2023, new data from the Ontario Securities Commission (OSC) shows.
In the results of a survey released on Tuesday, the OSC found that crypto ownership and awareness among Canadians had increased from that a few years ago. The survey polled 2,360 individuals age 18 and over between December 2025 and January 2026, finding that 59% of the respondents were aware of crypto assets and 25% held them.
“Crypto markets continue to evolve, and Canadians are participating in them more than ever before,” said Naizam Kanji, executive vice president of strategic regulation at the OSC. “By identifying emerging trends and behaviors with our research, we can look around corners, anticipate potential opportunities and risks, and ensure our regulatory approach supports investor protection while fostering fair and efficient markets.”
According to the survey, the results also suggested an increasing awareness of risk, though it was still based on a limited understanding of the industry. About 50% of crypto owners reported checking whether a platform was registered before using it, but many investors “had some misunderstanding around regulation, insurance protections and transaction capabilities.”
Lawmakers in Ottawa have proposed various measures to address different uses of cryptocurrency in the country. In April, the federal government advanced a bill that could ban political donations using crypto, and proposed banning digital asset ATMs, citing concerns about fraud.

title: Quantum Solutions loses top Japan ETH treasury spot after another $1.9 million sale
summary: The two sales have reduced Quantum’s ETH treasury holdings by 28.6% since mid-June and the firm has ceded the top Japanese ETH treasury spot.
full_text:
Quantum Solutions loses top Japan ETH treasury spot after another $1.9 million sale
Quick Take
- The two sales have reduced Quantum’s ETH treasury holdings by 28.6% since mid-June.
- The firm has now ceded the top Japanese ETH treasury spot to Def consulting.
We'd love your feedback.
Japan-listed Quantum Solutions sold another 1,000 ether (ETH) for approximately $1.9 million to help fund its AI data center expansion.
The company has now cut its ether holdings by nearly 30% since mid-June, simultaneously giving up its position as Japan's largest corporate ETH treasury.
GPT Pals Studio, a subsidiary of Quantum Solutions, sold the ether on Thursday at an average price of $1,903, according to a company filing. Quantum said it expects to recognize a loss of around $100,000 on the sale.
The transaction leaves Quantum Solutions with roughly 4,765 ETH, dropping it behind Def consulting, which holds 4,976 ETH, among publicly traded Japanese companies.
Quantum has now sold a total of 1,904 ETH in less than two months, nearly 29% of the 6,668.8 ETH it held before the sales. GPT Pals previously offloaded 904 ETH for approximately $1.6 million on June 16.
The company accumulated most of its ether during the fourth quarter 2025 crypto boom, when ETH was trading between roughly $4,000 and $4,500. Today, ETH is trading for $1,925, leaving the value of Quantum's remaining holdings at approximately $9.2 million.
Quantum said the proceeds are going to be used to support its AI infrastructure and data center business, including data center agreements and GPU equipment.
The company has also expanded the amount of ether authorized for sale from 1,875 ETH to 4,375 ETH. This means that Quantum may sell up to another 2,471 ETH through Oct. 30 following the previous sales of a combined 1,904 ETH.
However, 3,050 of its remaining holdings are pledged to a Singapore-based lender as collateral for an earlier borrowing, while 1,714.8 ETH is held in GPT Pals' crypto trading account. So the remaining sale authorization exceeds the unpledged holdings by over 750 ether.
Quantum would likely need to secure the release or replacement of some of the pledged collateral, or acquire additional ETH, to sell that full authorized amount.

title: JPMorgan says crypto bill’s fading odds hurt outlook, warns parts could discourage institutional adoption
summary: The falling odds of the Clarity Act passing the Senate before year-end are a setback for crypto markets, JPMorgan analysts said.
full_text:
JPMorgan says crypto bill's fading odds hurt outlook, warns parts could discourage institutional adoption
Quick Take
- The falling odds of the Clarity Act passing the Senate before year-end are a setback for crypto markets, JPMorgan analysts said.
- While the analysts see the legislation as broadly positive for crypto, they warned parts of the current draft could discourage institutional participation.
We'd love your feedback.
The falling odds of the Clarity Act passing the U.S. Senate before year-end are a setback for crypto markets, JPMorgan analysts said, adding that parts of the current draft of the crypto bill could discourage institutional participation.
Prediction market odds of the bill passing before year-end have fallen to 37%, the lowest implied probability this year, as the Senate prioritizes other legislation ahead of the summer recess, JPMorgan analysts led by managing director Nikolaos Panigirtzoglou said in a Wednesday report. The odds currently stand at 37% on Kalshi and 26% on Polymarket. Disagreements over ethics, enforcement, stablecoin yield, decentralized finance and illicit finance remain unresolved, the analysts noted.
The analysts have previously viewed the Clarity Act, or crypto market structure bill, as a positive catalyst for crypto because it would create a clearer regulatory framework for the industry. Under the legislation, digital commodities would be overseen by the Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC), while digital securities would remain under the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC).
If the bill is eventually passed, it would support the development of more institutional-grade market infrastructure, ease regulatory constraints around decentralized finance and stablecoin issuers, increase onshore liquidity and trading volumes as activity gradually shifts from offshore venues to U.S.-compliant markets, and lower barriers for brokerages, exchanges, market makers, custodians and bank-affiliated platforms to enter the crypto industry, the analysts said.
However, the analysts said parts of the current draft could discourage institutional participation rather than promote it.
"One example is if DeFi is able to trade tokenized securities and tokenized derivatives entirely outside of SEC or CFTC jurisdiction, which the bill as currently drafted would allow. A second example is if crypto entities have to do little if any AML for performing the same activities as banks and broker dealers," the analysts said.
Overall, the longer approval of the Clarity Act is postponed, the greater the risk that growth in tokenization and blockchain-based financial applications is absorbed by existing financial infrastructure instead of benefiting public crypto networks, the analysts said.
The U.S. House of Representatives passed the Clarity Act last July, but the bill has since stalled in the Senate amid disagreements over stablecoin yields, crypto disclosure requirements and other provisions. Senators are working on bipartisan revisions ahead of the Senate's August summer recess, though a vote is expected to slip until after lawmakers return in mid-September.
Earlier Thursday, Crypto Council for Innovation published a 35-page report calling for crypto market structure legislation to be passed without further delay. "A failure to act now will cede the United States' historic leadership of market regulation and innovation to other jurisdictions and will threaten U.S. dollar dominance," the council said.
